readings.c1s1:
¶
'''timely''' (tīm′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''timliche''; < ''timely'', ''a.''] 1. Early; soon.

{{smaller block|He did command me to call ''timely'' on him.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, ii. 3. 51.}}}}

2. In good time; opportunely.

{{smaller block|These, when their black crimes they went about,
First ''timely'' charmed their useless conscience out.
{{right|''Dryden'', Astræa Redux, l. 190.}}}}

{{smaller block|You have rebuk'd me ''timely'', and most friendly.
{{right|''Brome'', Jovial Crew, ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|The next Imposture may not be so ''timely'' detected.
{{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, v. 6.}}}}

3†. Leisurely.

'''timely-parted''' (tīm′li-pär″ted), ''a.'' Having died a natural death. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Oft have I seen a ''timely-parted'' ghost,
Of ashy semblance, meagre, pale, and bloodless; . . .
But see, his face is black and full of blood, . . .
It cannot be but he was murder'd here.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 161.}}}}
readings.c1s2:
¶
'''timenog''', ''n.'' Same as ''timenoguy''.

'''timenoguy''' (tī-men′ọ̄-gī), ''n.'' [Also ''timenog''; origin obscure. The form ''timenoguy'' appar. simulates ''guy''<sup>1</sup>.] ''Naut.'', a rope stretched from one place to another to prevent gear from getting foul; especially, a rope made fast to the stock of the waist-anchor, to keep the tacks and sheets from fouling on the stock.

'''timeous, timeously.''' See ''timous, timously''.

'''timepiece''' (tīm′pēs), ''n.'' Any machine or apparatus by which the progress of time is recorded, as a clepsydra or a time-candle; in ordinary use, a watch or clock.

'''time-pleaser''' (tīm′plē″zėr), ''n.'' One who complies with the prevailing opinions of the time, whatever they may be.

{{smaller block|Scandal'd the suppliants for the people, call'd them ''Time-pleasers'', flatterers, foes to nobleness.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 1. 45.}}}}

'''timer''' (tī′mėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who keeps or measures and records time; a timekeeper.

{{smaller block|To make a record in this country requires the presence of three ''timers'' or measurers, and two of these must agree, or the intermediate one of the three be taken as the correct one.
{{right|''The Century'', XL. 205.}}}}
readings.c1s4:
¶
{{smaller block|Trimming and ''time-serving'' . . . are but two words for the same thing.
{{right|''South.''}}}}

'''time-serving''' (tīm′sėr″ving), ''a.'' Characterized by an obsequious or too ready compliance with the times, and especially with the will or humors of those in authority; obsequious; truckling.

'''time-servingness''' (tīm′sėr″ving-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being time-serving. ''Roger North.''

'''time-sight''' (tīm′sīt), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', an observation of the altitude of any heavenly body for the purpose of deducing the time and consequently the longitude.

'''time-signal''' (tīm′sig″na̤l), ''n.'' A signal operated from an observatory to indicate the time of day to persons at distant points.

'''time-signature''' (tīm′sig″nạ̄-tụ̄r), ''n.'' In ''musical notation'', same as ''rhythmical signature'' (which see, under ''rhythmical'').

'''time-table''' (tīm′tā″bl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A tabular statement or scheme, showing the time when certain things are to take place or be attended: as, a school ''time-table'', showing the hours for study
readings.c2s2:
the relative duration indicated by a note. See ''note''<sup>1</sup>, ''rhythm'', and ''meter''<sup>2</sup>.

'''time-work''' (tīm′wėrk), ''n.'' Labor paid for by the day or the hour, in opposition to ''piece-work'', or labor paid for by the amount produced.

'''timid''' (tim′id), ''a.'' [< F. ''timide'' = Sp. ''tímido'' = Pg. It. ''timido,'' < L. ''timidus,'' full of fear, fearful, timid, < ''timere,'' fear.] Fearful; easily alarmed; timorous; shy.

{{smaller block|Poor is the triumph o'er the ''timid'' hare.
{{right|''Thomson'', Autumn, l. 401.}}}}

{{smaller block|A ''timid'' creature, lax of knee and hip,
Whom small disturbance whitens round the lip.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', The Moral Bully.}}}}

'''timidity''' (ti-mid′ị-ti), ''n.'' [< F. ''timidité'' = It. ''timidità,'' < L. ''timidita(-t)s,'' fearfulness, timidness, < ''timidus,'' fearful, timid: see ''timid.''] The character of being timid, or easily frightened or daunted; cowardice; fearfulness; timorousness; shyness.

{{smaller block|This proceedeth from nothing else but extreame folly and ''timidity'' of heart.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 234.}}}}

{{smaller block|"Viglius," wrote Margaret to Philip, "is so much afraid of being cut to pieces that his ''timidity'' has become incredible."
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, I. 574.}}}}

=''Syn.'' See ''bashfulness.''

'''timidly''' (tim′id-li), ''adv.'' In a timid or apprehensive manner; without boldness.

'''timidness''' (tim′id-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being timid; timidity.

'''timidous†''' (tim′i-dus), ''a.'' [< L. ''timidus,'' timid: see ''timid.''] Timid.

{{smaller block|His lordship knew him to be a mere lawyer, and a ''timidous'' man.
{{right|''Roger North'', Lord Guilford, II. 31. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''timmen''' (tim′en), ''n.'' [A var. of (or error for?) ''tammin'', ''tamin''.] Same as ''tamin'', 1.

readings.c3s3:
Sp. Pg. ''temeroso'' = It. ''timoroso'', < ML. ''timorosus'', fearful, < L. ''timor'', fear, < ''timere'', fear: see ''timid.''] 1. Fearful; timid; shy; shrinking.

{{smaller block|They were wont to be very ''timorous'' and fearful upon the sea, nor to venture upon it but only in the summer time.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}}}}

{{smaller block|Like a ''timorous'' thief, most fain would steal
What law does vouch mine own.
{{right|''Shak.'', All's Well, ii. 5. 86.}}}}

2. Betokening or proceeding from lack of boldness or courage; characterized by fear; weakly hesitant: as, ''timorous'' doubts.

{{smaller block|''Rod.'' Here is her father's house; I'll call aloud.
''Iago.'' Do, with like ''timorous'' accent and dire yell
As when . . . the fire
Is spied in populous cities.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 1. 75.}}}}

{{smaller block|Against all ''timorous'' counsels he [Lincoln] had the courage to seize the moment.
{{right|''Emerson'', Emancipation Proclamation.}}}}

¶
'''timorously''' (tim′ọ̄-rus-li), ''adv.'' In a timorous manner; fearfully; timidly; without boldness or confidence.

'''timorousness''' (tim′ọ̄-rus-nes), ''n.'' The state of being timorous; timidity; want of courage.

{{smaller block|''Timorousness'' is called caution, rashness is called quickness of spirit, covetousness is frugality.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 846.}}}}

'''timorsome''' (tim′ọr-sum), ''a.'' [Also ''timoursum'', ''timersome'', ''timmersome''; an accom. form of ''timorous'', as if < L. ''timor'', fear (see ''timorous''), + ''-some''.] Easily frightened; timid. ''Scott'', Pirate, xviii. [Scotch.]
